<context ref="file:///Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/YFL/yfl-personal-expense-tracker/docs/demo-seed.md">
# Demo Data Seed

A re-runnable script that populates a self-contained **"Sample Family (DEMO)"**
in the **remote** Supabase project, so the running app can be logged into for
documentation screenshots/videos and manual exploratory testing.

It is deliberately **image-free**: every seeded receipt has
`receipt_image_path = null`, so receipts render in their placeholder state
("No image" / "(manual)"). See the note on that below.

> **Reuse:** the seed is written so a future automated test harness can reuse
> the same fixtures. That harness is **not** built yet — this is a dev utility
> today.

## Logins

| Role   | Email                        |
| ------ | ---------------------------- |
| Owner  | `sample.parent@example.com`  |
| Member | `sample.partner@example.com` |

Both share one family and one **randomly generated password**, printed to the
console at the end of each seed run (nothing memorable is left standing in the
project). Copy it from the run output. `@example.com` is an IANA-reserved
documentation domain — it accepts no mail and can't collide with real accounts.

## Commands

```bash
npm run seed:demo            # auto-clean any prior demo data, then rebuild
npm run seed:demo:teardown   # delete the demo users + demo family
```

Both wrap `op run --env-file=.env -- tsx …`, so the required env is pulled from
1Password just like `npm run dev`. They need:

- `PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` — the target project (echoed on start).
- `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` — full-access secret; required to create the auth
  users (Admin API) and to insert RLS-protected rows. The scripts hard-fail with
  a clear message if either is missing.

`seed:demo` is **auto-clean-then-recreate**: it runs the teardown first, so every
run yields the same known-good state. Deletion is scoped strictly to the two
demo emails and the `Sample Family (DEMO)` name, so it can only ever touch demo
artifacts — never your real data (which lives under a different `family_id` and
stays invisible to the demo login via RLS, and vice-versa).

## What it creates

- **Two auth users** (owner + member), one shared **family**, with the app's own
  **default categories + spending hierarchy** (via the `create_default_categories`
  and `create_default_hierarchy` RPCs) so the demo matches a real new family.
- **~150 receipts** spread across **all of 2025 + Jan–Jul 2026**, ~6–8 per month,
  split across both users and most of the 13 default groupings / 3 Areas of
  Importance — enough to fill the Spending grid, YTD, and the compare-to-prior-year
  toggle.
- **~95 transactions**, most matched 1:1 to a receipt (equal amount, date within
  3 days), the rest unmatched on each side.
- **One instance of every notable edge state**, planted in recent months so it's
  visible without scrolling: split receipt, matched pair, unmatched (both sides),
  duplicate pair, suspicious/old date, future-dated ("Upcoming"), refund/credit,
  excluded transaction, amount-not-read (null total), foreign currency (USD), and
  uncategorized.

The dataset is generated deterministically (fixed RNG seed), so reseeding
produces the same data and screenshots stay stable.

## The no-image consequence

Because no receipt has an image, every screen shows its empty/placeholder state:
the Expenses page shows a column of grey "No image" boxes, the Receipts page has
blank thumbnail cells, and Reconciliation tags every receipt "(manual)". This is
intentional. If a screenshot ever needs the receipt-image viewer itself, seed a
few receipts with real placeholder images (a small change to `scripts/demo/data.ts`).

## Files

- `scripts/demo/common.ts` — env guard, service-role client, teardown.
- `scripts/demo/data.ts` — pure, deterministic dataset generator (no DB access).
- `scripts/demo/seed.ts` — orchestrates users → family → categories → data.
- `scripts/demo/teardown.ts` — standalone teardown entrypoint.

Run via `tsx` (added as a dev dependency).

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).

- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

`docs/demo-seed.md` isn't a data file — it documents a seeding *program* (`scripts/demo/*.ts`). Nothing gets "uploaded" as a file; the script talks to Supabase's REST + Admin APIs with the service-role key and inserts rows directly. Here's the whole picture.

## The one command

```bash
npm run seed:demo
```

That expands to `op run --env-file=.env -- tsx scripts/demo/seed.ts`.

I verified the prerequisites are all in place already:

| Need | Status |
| --- | --- |
| `tsx` dev dependency | ✓ installed (`node_modules/tsx`) |
| `op` CLI (1Password) | ✓ `/usr/local/bin/op` |
| `PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` in `.env` | ✓ `https://acepytsyfbfhbwraswqj.supabase.co` |
| `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` in `.env` | ✓ present |
| `create_default_categories` / `create_default_hierarchy` RPCs | ✓ defined in `supabase/migrations/` |

Note that `package.json` + `scripts/` are still uncommitted, so this only works from this working tree.

## ⚠️ It writes to your live project

`PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` points at the real hosted project, so `npm run seed:demo` inserts ~245 rows (150 receipts, 95 transactions, plus 2 auth users and a family) into **production**. There's no local alternative right now — Docker isn't running, so there's no local Supabase to point at.

The isolation argument in the doc is sound: everything is scoped to a new `family_id`, and RLS keeps it invisible from your real login and vice-versa. `seed.ts:69` also auto-runs teardown first, and `teardownDemo()` (`scripts/demo/common.ts:89`) only ever deletes users matching the two `@example.com` emails and families named exactly `Sample Family (DEMO)`. So it's safe, but it is your production database.

## What actually happens, in order

`scripts/demo/seed.ts` does this — each step is a separate API call, so a failure leaves you partway through:

1. Echoes the target host (`Demo seed → target: acepytsyfbfhbwraswqj.supabase.co`) — read this line before letting it continue.
2. Teardown of any prior demo artifacts.
3. Creates the two auth users via the Admin API with `email_confirm: true` (so no confirmation mail is sent), sharing one freshly generated 20-char password.
4. Inserts the `families` row + two `family_members` rows.
5. Calls the two RPCs so the demo family gets the same default categories and spending hierarchy a real new family gets.
6. `generateDemoData()` (`scripts/demo/data.ts`, pure — no DB access) builds the rows deterministically, then they're inserted into `transactions`, `receipts`, `expense_categories` in 500-row chunks.

## Getting in afterwards

The **password is printed once, at the end of the run, and is never stored** — copy it out of the terminal before you lose the scrollback. Then:

```bash
npm run dev   # log in at http://localhost:5173/login
```

as `sample.parent@example.com` (owner) or `sample.partner@example.com` (member).

## Cleaning up

```bash
npm run seed:demo:teardown
```

Deleting the auth users cascades their receipts/categorizations/memberships; deleting the family cascades its transactions and category tables — between the two, nothing is left behind.

## If it fails

- **"Missing required env var(s)"** — `op` didn't resolve the `op://` references; check you're signed in (`op signin`).
- **`create_default_categories failed`** — the remote is behind on migrations; check with `supabase migration list`.
- **Users exist but the family insert fails** — just re-run `npm run seed:demo`; the auto-teardown at the top makes it idempotent.

Migrations are fully in sync, so that risk is cleared — and the `.env` FIFO makes sense now.

But checking the RPC grants turned up a likely blocker in the seed:

```sql
-- supabase/migrations/20260717_security_remediation_chain.sql:199
REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.create_default_hierarchy(uuid) FROM PUBLIC;
GRANT   EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.create_default_hierarchy(uuid) TO authenticated;

REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.create_default_categories(uuid) FROM PUBLIC;
GRANT   EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.create_default_categories(uuid) TO authenticated, service_role;
```

`create_default_categories` names `service_role` explicitly; `create_default_hierarchy` doesn't. Before that migration, both were callable by anyone via the implicit `PUBLIC` grant. After it, only `authenticated` can call the hierarchy one — and `service_role` is not a member of `authenticated` in Supabase, so the grant doesn't cascade. `BYPASSRLS` doesn't help either; EXECUTE is a separate privilege.

The seed runs entirely as `service_role`, so `seed.ts:98` will very likely die with `permission denied for function create_default_hierarchy`, right after creating the users and family:

```ts
const { error: hierErr } = await admin.rpc('create_default_hierarchy', { p_family_id: familyId });
```

Note the function *body* is fine — the comment at line 196 says the guard deliberately allows the `auth.uid() IS NULL` migration/owner path, which is exactly how service-role calls arrive. It's purely the missing grant.

I'd call this likely rather than certain; the cheapest way to settle it is just to run `npm run seed:demo`. Failure there is self-cleaning — you'd be left with the two demo users and an empty family, and the next run's auto-teardown wipes them before rebuilding.

Two ways forward:

1. **New migration** adding `GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.create_default_hierarchy(uuid) TO service_role;` — restores the symmetry that 20260717 seems to have missed, and doesn't reopen the `anon` path that migration was closing.
2. **Keep the grant as-is** and have `seed.ts` insert the `importance_areas` / `category_groups` rows directly instead of calling the RPC — no schema change, but the seed then duplicates hierarchy logic it currently gets for free.

I'd go with (1): it's one line, and the asymmetry with `create_default_categories` on the adjacent line reads like an oversight rather than a deliberate restriction.

-- Function: create_default_hierarchy(family_id)
-- Idempotent seed of Importance areas + Groupings, then maps the default
-- categories into Groupings by name. Categories whose names aren't in the map
-- (custom or renamed) stay group_id NULL and surface as Uncategorized.
--
-- Called for every existing family below, and by the app (rpc) for new families.
-- ============================================================================

RETURNS VOID AS $$
DECLARE

That changes the recommendation — and surfaces a second coupling I should flag before you decide.

## If the list is going to churn, there are *two* SQL copies to keep in step, not one

1. **`create_default_categories` RPC** — a verbatim duplicate of the 43 names+colors. Nothing in `src/` calls it; only your new `seed.ts` does. Every refinement to `DEFAULT_CATEGORIES` silently desyncs it.

2. **The name→group map inside `create_default_hierarchy`** (`20260709_spending_hierarchy.sql:167+`) — this one is easy to miss. It assigns `group_id` by matching category names as string literals. Rename `Coffee and Tea`, or add a new category, and it falls through the map to `group_id NULL` — which the spending report renders as **Uncategorized**. The function's own comment says exactly that: *"Categories whose names aren't in the map (custom or renamed) stay group_id NULL and surface as Uncategorized."*

So today, refining the TS list quietly degrades the Spending grid for every family created afterwards, unless you also ship a migration editing the SQL map. That coupling isn't documented anywhere and there's no test guarding it.

## The shape that survives churn

Put the grouping on the TS constant, next to name and color:

```ts
{ name: 'Coffee and Tea', color: '#92400E', group: 'Everyday' }
```

# Demo Data Seed

A re-runnable script that populates a self-contained **"Sample Family (DEMO)"**
in the **remote** Supabase project, so the running app can be logged into for
documentation screenshots/videos and manual exploratory testing.

It is deliberately **image-free**: every seeded receipt has
`receipt_image_path = null`, so receipts render in their placeholder state
("No image" / "(manual)"). See the note on that below.

> **Reuse:** the seed is written so a future automated test harness can reuse
> the same fixtures. That harness is **not** built yet — this is a dev utility
> today.

## Logins

| Role   | Email                        |
| ------ | ---------------------------- |
| Owner  | `sample.parent@example.com`  |
| Member | `sample.partner@example.com` |

Both share one family and one **randomly generated password**, printed to the
console at the end of each seed run (nothing memorable is left standing in the
project). Copy it from the run output. `@example.com` is an IANA-reserved
documentation domain — it accepts no mail and can't collide with real accounts.

## Commands

```bash
npm run seed:demo            # auto-clean any prior demo data, then rebuild
npm run seed:demo:teardown   # delete the demo users + demo family
```

Both wrap `op run --env-file=.env -- tsx …`, so the required env is pulled from
1Password just like `npm run dev`. They need:

- `PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` — the target project (echoed on start).
- `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` — full-access secret; required to create the auth
  users (Admin API) and to insert RLS-protected rows. The scripts hard-fail with
  a clear message if either is missing.

`seed:demo` is **auto-clean-then-recreate**: it runs the teardown first, so every
run yields the same known-good state. Deletion is scoped strictly to the two
demo emails and the `Sample Family (DEMO)` name, so it can only ever touch demo
artifacts — never your real data (which lives under a different `family_id` and
stays invisible to the demo login via RLS, and vice-versa).

## What it creates

- **Two auth users** (owner + member), one shared **family**, with the app's own
  **default categories + spending hierarchy** (via the `create_default_categories`
  and `create_default_hierarchy` RPCs) so the demo matches a real new family.
- **~150 receipts** spread across **all of 2025 + Jan–Jul 2026**, ~6–8 per month,
  split across both users and most of the 13 default groupings / 3 Areas of
  Importance — enough to fill the Spending grid, YTD, and the compare-to-prior-year
  toggle.
- **~95 transactions**, most matched 1:1 to a receipt (equal amount, date within
  3 days), the rest unmatched on each side.
- **One instance of every notable edge state**, planted in recent months so it's
  visible without scrolling: split receipt, matched pair, unmatched (both sides),
  duplicate pair, suspicious/old date, future-dated ("Upcoming"), refund/credit,
  excluded transaction, amount-not-read (null total), foreign currency (USD), and
  uncategorized.

The dataset is generated deterministically (fixed RNG seed), so reseeding
produces the same data and screenshots stay stable.

## The no-image consequence

Because no receipt has an image, every screen shows its empty/placeholder state:
the Expenses page shows a column of grey "No image" boxes, the Receipts page has
blank thumbnail cells, and Reconciliation tags every receipt "(manual)". This is
intentional. If a screenshot ever needs the receipt-image viewer itself, seed a
few receipts with real placeholder images (a small change to `scripts/demo/data.ts`).

## Files

- `scripts/demo/common.ts` — env guard, service-role client, teardown.
- `scripts/demo/data.ts` — pure, deterministic dataset generator (no DB access).

Code changes are done and the migration is live. The seed run is **blocked** — but not by anything in the code.

## Blocker: the service-role key is empty in 1Password

```
✗ Demo seed failed: Missing required env var(s): SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY.
```

Your `.env` is a 1Password *Environments* file (`# This file was generated by 1Password` — that's also why it's a FIFO, it's served live rather than stored). Every value in it is an already-resolved literal, not an `op://` reference. Five of the six have values; `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` is declared but **empty**.

So the fix is in 1Password, not the repo: open the **"YFL Expense App"** environment and paste in the service-role key from the Supabase dashboard (Project Settings → API Keys → `service_role`). Then `npm run seed:demo` should go. I've left everything staged for that — nothing else needs doing first.

## Correction on the grant

My earlier "the seed will very likely fail with permission denied" was wrong. `docs/product-backlog.md:36` records the opposite behaviour from live testing: on Supabase, `REVOKE … FROM PUBLIC` doesn't remove `anon`/`authenticated`/`service_role`, because they hold *direct* grants from default privileges. `service_role` therefore never lost EXECUTE on `create_default_hierarchy`, and the seed would have run fine as-is.

I kept the grant anyway and wrote it as hardening rather than a fix — relying on an unstated default privilege is exactly the fragility that produced the F3 follow-up migration. The migration comment says so explicitly.

## What changed

**`supabase/migrations/20260726_default_seed_function_cleanup.sql`** (new, applied to remote):
- `GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.create_default_hierarchy(uuid) TO service_role;`
- `DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS public.create_default_categories(uuid);`

**`scripts/demo/seed.ts:96`** — the two RPCs became:

```ts
const categoryService = new CategoryService(admin);
await categoryService.createDefaultCategories(familyId);
await categoryService.createDefaultHierarchy(familyId);
```

**`scripts/demo/data.ts:26`** and **`docs/demo-seed.md`** — updated the references to the dropped RPC.

Verified: `supabase db push` applied cleanly; Prettier passes on all three files. The run also proved the one risky bit of the seed change — importing `CategoryService` into a plain `tsx` script works, because its `$lib` imports are all `import type` and get erased at transpile. The failure came later, at `readConfig()`.

Two things I noticed but didn't touch:

- **`scripts/` isn't type-checked.** The generated tsconfig's `include` covers `src`, `test`, `tests` — not `scripts`. So `npm run check` never sees the seed code. Worth a backlog line if you want it covered.
- I haven't committed anything, per your rules. `scripts/`, the new migration, `package.json`, and the two doc edits are all sitting uncommitted.
